title: Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Write two functions. serialize turns a binary tree into a string, and deserialize turns that string back into the same tree. You choose the format. The only rule is that deserialize(serialize(tree)) gives back an identical tree, including empty spots.

example.caption: Preorder with a # for every missing child. Reading the string left to right rebuilds the tree.

output.label: serialized string, split at the commas

idea.sentence: Write the tree in preorder and put a marker for every missing child, so the string alone says exactly where each subtree ends.

jargon.plain: Turn an in-memory structure into text (or bytes) that you could store or send.
A placeholder written for a missing child. Without it, the string would not say which side a lone child is on.

watch.inputHint: One argument: the tree as a level-order list. The driver serializes it, deserializes the string, and shows the rebuilt tree as a list. It should equal the input.

compare.bruteLabel: Join strings with + on every node

rows.name: Append to one growing string
rows.note: In languages where a string append copies, each append re-copies the text so far.

rows.name: Preorder tokens with #
rows.note: n nodes and n + 1 markers give 2n + 1 tokens. Both functions touch each token once.

fast.takeaway: A tree with n nodes has n + 1 empty spots. Preorder plus a marker for each is one token per spot or node, read back in the same order.

stages.title: Write # for empty
stages.note: A missing child is written as #. This is what lets the reader know a subtree has ended.

stages.title: Write node, left, right
stages.note: Write the node's value, then serialize the left subtree, then the right subtree.

stages.title: Join the tokens
stages.note: Join all tokens with commas to get the final string.

stages.title: Split into tokens
stages.note: deserialize starts by splitting the string at the commas and keeping a position next.

stages.title: Read a token
stages.note: Take the next token. # means null. Otherwise make a node, then read its left subtree, then its right subtree. The order is the same as when writing.

edges.title: Empty tree
edges.why: serialize gives just "#". deserialize reads that single marker and returns null.

edges.title: Single node
edges.why: The string is "1,#,#": the node and one marker for each missing child.

edges.title: Left chain
edges.why: The markers keep every child on the right side, so a lone left child stays a left child.

edges.title: Negative values
edges.why: The comma is the separator, so "-1" is one token. A minus sign never clashes with the # marker.

gotchas.text: Preorder alone is not enough. Without markers, 1,2,3 could be many different trees. The # tokens are what make the string unambiguous.
Read in the same order you wrote: node, then left, then right. Reading right before left would build a mirror image.
Use a separator. Without commas, the values 1 and 23 would look like 12 and 3.
Number(token) converts "-5" correctly. Check for '#' before converting, because Number('#') is NaN and would sneak in as a value.
strconv.Atoi returns an error as its second value. Ignoring it is fine here only because the tokens came from serialize. Real input would need checking.

recap.key: Write node, left, right with # for empty. Read the tokens back in the same order with a shared position.
moves: serialize: # for null, else value, left, right
deserialize: split, keep a shared next position
Read a token: # is null, else node, left, right
